extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and researchers interested in media, propaganda, hate speech, and genocide
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize and identify forms, mechanisms, and legal thresholds of media that promote hatred or contribute to genocide. Useful for recognizing propaganda techniques, modes of dissemination, and when media conduct may meet national or international prosecutable standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of hate media
rubrics_metrics.description: Media that contributes to the demonization and stigmatization of people who belong to different groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided include Radio Televizija Srbije, Radio Télévision Libre des Mille Collines (RTLM), and Der Stürmer; the definition emphasizes contribution to demonization and stigmatization rather than merely disagreeable content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecutability of hate speech under national law
rubrics_metrics.description: Hate speech that is promoted by media can be prosecuted by national laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes national prosecution is possible for hate speech; separate international standards apply where media contributes to genocide.

rubrics_metrics.name: When hate media is an international crime (incitement to genocide / crime against humanity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hate-media used to foment the cleansing of a particular national, ethnic, racial or religious group, in whole or in part, can be prosecuted for inciting genocide under international law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At Nuremberg incitement to genocide was declared a crime against humanity, though early definitions focused on calls for direct extermination; definitions were later modified (e.g., ICTR) to include broader forms of incitement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements of hate-media propaganda as crime against humanity (direct & indirect incitement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hate-media propaganda considered a crime against humanity must be involved in the direct and indirect incitement of genocide defined as 'directly provoking the perpetrator(s) to commit genocide' by various communicative means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modes cited include speeches, shouting, threats in public spaces or gatherings, sale or dissemination of written material or printed matter, public display of placards or posters, or other means of audiovisual communication. The text quotes this formulation from ICTR-related definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of disinformation and fabricated content to provoke violence
rubrics_metrics.description: Fabrication and disinformation in broadcasts (e.g., fabricated conversations or false reports of atrocities) that are presented as factual and blamed on another group to provoke attacks or displacement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: testimony at Milošević's trial described fabricated conversations and television broadcasts of corpses falsely attributed to another group; clandestine operations blamed on target groups are cited as mechanisms of hate media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propaganda speeches and communications as instigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Speeches, communications, acts, or omissions by public figures or media figures that contribute to perpetrators' decisions to commit crimes can be treated as instigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: indictment against Vojislav Šešelj charged that his speeches and communications 'contributed to the perpetrators' decision to commit the crimes alleged.' This highlights that both direct messages and broader communicative conduct can support criminal charges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Issuing explicit instructions or orders to commit violence
rubrics_metrics.description: Media that issues instructions or orders to commit violence or killing increases culpability for incitement to genocide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: RTLM is noted for telling 'all citizens to see killing Tutsis as their responsibility' and for issuing instructions/orders to commit genocide; RTLM founders were sentenced by the ICTR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of hateful language, caricature, and false accusations to demonize groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of extreme hateful language, grotesque caricatures, and false accusations to demonize a target group constitutes a core technique of hate media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Der Stürmer is cited as using these methods to promote racial ideology and incite violence; such content vilifies targets and promulgates stereotypes, contributing to mass acceptance of persecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Targeting and tailoring propaganda to specific audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: Distributing hateful content tailored to particular audience segments (e.g., working-class or less-educated populations) to shape public opinion and increase influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Der Stürmer was aimed at the general German public, particularly the working class, and its wide distribution made it influential; the article implies audience targeting and distribution strategies magnify impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media's role in spurring, directing, and facilitating killings
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond persuasion, hate media can play an active role in spurring and directing killings, particularly in areas already predisposed to violence or where resistance exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: RTLM is described as helping to 'spur and direct killings' and as creating groundwork that 'literally drive[s] on the killing once the genocide started' — illustrating how media can move from rhetoric to coordination and facilitation of mass violence.
